# Khandha Saṁyutta (SN 22)
**ID:** SN 22
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
Doctrinally, the samyutta treats the five aggregates (*khandha*: form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness), predominantly defined as the "aggregates connected with grasping" (*upādānakkhandha*) [SuttaCentral]. The texts explore how the aggregates act as the objects, functional supports, stimulants, and products of clinging, emphasizing the marks of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*) to dismantle theories of a permanent soul [SuttaCentral]. Prominent among these is the *Anattalakkhaṇasutta* (SN 22.59), the traditional second sermon delivered to the group of five monks [Allon, Senior Manuscripts; SuttaCentral]. The collection features both highly abbreviated formulaic templates and vivid narrative accounts illustrating the application of the aggregates to meditation, theoretical debates on personal identity, and guidance during severe illness and dying [SuttaCentral].
Extensive parallels to the *Khandhasaṁyutta* exist across early Buddhist literature. SuttaCentral records parallels for 102 discourses, most prominently 89 suttas in the Chinese *Saṁyukta-āgama* (T 99), as well as discourses in the *Ekottarika-āgama*, *Madhyama-āgama*, and Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā* [SuttaCentral]. Several individual suttas are preserved in Gāndhārī birch-bark scrolls from the British Library and Senior collections, including parallels to the *Natumhākasutta* (SN 22.33), the *Vāsijaṭasutta* (SN 22.101), and the *Kulaputtenadukkhāsutta* (SN 22.146) [Glass, Connected Discourses in Gandhāra]. Sanskrit fragments and Vinaya parallels (such as the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra*) also preserve cognates to the second sermon and related texts [Allon, Senior Manuscripts; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus demonstrates heavy cross-language alignment with T 99 and the Tibetan *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā* (D 4094), agreeing with SuttaCentral's curated parallels, while Pali-internal reuse registers over 70,000 matches with other canonical texts, sharing major textual templates with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), *Diṭṭhi Saṁyutta* (SN 24), and the Vinaya *Mahākhandhaka* [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral].
